headline: High risk of capability conflict and cascading error: ECC can write/modify shared state while awesome-python is a non-runnable docs-only collection, making the pair unsafe if wired together.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No direct shared channel is documented, so prompt injection is not default. However, ECC can use MCP, stdin/stdout, and filesystem surfaces, while awesome-python is a docs-only repository that could be manually copied into ECC workflows. That makes manual or file-based instruction smuggling plausible, but only with unusual bridging.
conditions: IF the operator copies content from awesome-python into ECC prompts or MCP inputs, injection becomes possible.
IF ECC is configured to ingest repository text as instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer behavior.
mitigations: Keep awesome-python content read-only and out of prompt context.
Disable MCP ingestion for untrusted text sources.
Use a fixed prompt template that strips instructions from copied content.
Review any pasted repository text before sending it to ECC.

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-python touches no data classes and has no network egress, so it is not a leakage source. ECC does touch session summaries, skills, hooks, git history, and security findings, and it can write files and call APIs. The pair can leak only if sensitive material is placed into ECC-managed state or shared files, so the blast radius is limited and configuration-dependent.
conditions: IF sensitive data is stored in ECC session files or hooks, ECC may expose it through its API calls or file writes.
IF the operator places secrets into shared workspace files, ECC can read and persist them.
mitigations: Avoid storing secrets in ECC session summaries or skills.
Restrict ECC file access to a dedicated workspace.
Rotate any secrets accidentally written into ECC-managed files.
Audit API destinations before enabling sync features.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC has unrestricted write, git, shell, and network capabilities, plus shared-state warnings for multiple instances. awesome-python is non-runnable and has no write surface, but if the pair is used in the same workspace, ECC can overwrite or mutate repository state without coordination. The conflict risk is high because defaults allow destructive writes and git changes.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same checkout or config directory, ECC can overwrite files or git state.
IF ECC runs alongside another instance without a separate root, session files may collide.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent.
Set a distinct root for ECC before running multiple instances.
Make the repository read-only for ECC when not editing.
Snapshot the workspace before allowing git writes.
Pause one agent while the other mutates shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: awesome-python is a curated collection, so its outputs are likely treated as reference material, while ECC is built around skills, hooks, and agent definitions that can operationalize inputs. If ECC consumes repository-derived guidance without verification, a mistaken or stale recommendation can cascade into file edits, package installs, or GitHub actions. The pathway exists, but not every default flow is fully automated.
conditions: IF ECC uses repository text as authoritative guidance, it may act on incorrect or stale instructions.
IF ECC turns copied recommendations into installs or git changes without review, errors cascade downstream.
mitigations: Require human review before ECC executes repository-derived actions.
Mark awesome-python content as advisory, not authoritative.
Disable auto-apply for installs and git commits.
Add a verification step before any external API call.

E_compliance.rationale: No explicit residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for either agent, and awesome-python touches no regulated data classes. ECC does handle session summaries, hooks, and security findings, so compliance concerns arise only if the operator stores regulated data in those surfaces. Because the pair itself does not mandate such data flow, the risk is low.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in ECC session summaries or hooks, retention and residency controls must be checked.
IF the operator routes EU or PHI data through ECC-managed files, compliance review is required.
mitigations: Do not place regulated data in ECC-managed files.
Review retention settings before enabling persistence.
Keep compliance-sensitive workflows outside ECC.
Document any data-class changes before rollout.
